memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "'Eat it in the sanctuary area, because it is your share and your sons' share of the food offerings presented to the LORD; for so I have been commanded. But you and your sons and your daughters may eat the breast that was waved and the thigh that was presented. Eat them in a ceremonially clean place; they are given to you and your children as your share of the Israelites' fellowship offerings.'" - Lev 10:13-14 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
Your share. Moses says it twice.

On a day when Aaron has lost more than he can measure, God reminds him what still belongs to him. The priesthood continues. The provision continues. Two sons remain, and daughters, and a portion set aside by God's own command.

Grief has a way of eclipsing everything. When something enormous is taken, the losses fill the whole horizon and what remains becomes invisible.

It is not cruelty to point at what is left. It is mercy.

Jeremiah, in the middle of Lamentations — a book of raw national grief — writes: I say to myself, "The LORD is my portion; therefore I will wait for him" (Lam 3:24). He does not deny the devastation. He names what he still has.

David wrote, LORD, you alone are my portion and my cup; you make my lot secure (Ps 16:5).

If you have lost something significant, this is not a call to pretend it does not hurt. It is an invitation, when you are able, to look also at what God has not taken.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. Has a loss made me blind to what God has left in my hands?
2. What is my "share" — what has God given me that remains?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Father, help me to grieve honestly and still to see what You have given me. You Yourself are my portion. Amen.
